analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Conditions Survey found that 23.5% of firms in health care and social assistance used AI in the most recent measurement period, up from 22.0% in the prior period, making this one of the more consistently measured sectors in the survey. That incremental rise suggests steady rather than dramatic uptake across a broad industry that ranges from large hospital systems to small social service providers, so the headline figure almost certainly masks wide variation between well-resourced academic medical centers and smaller community practices.

On the infrastructure side, NIH anchors the research foundation that clinical AI is built on, making biomedical data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable under what it describes as FAIR principles, and funding the datasets and methods that underlie model development across electronic health records, omics, imaging, and disease-specific repositories. That public investment shapes what private developers can train on, which in turn shapes what eventually reaches clinical settings.

Model quality in health contexts is gaining a more disciplined measurement framework. OpenAI introduced HealthBench, a benchmark built with 262 physicians practicing across 60 countries, covering 5,000 realistic health conversations each graded against physician-written rubrics, with 48,562 unique criteria in total. The benchmark found that o3 outperforms other tested models including Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro, and that OpenAI's frontier models improved by 28% on HealthBench in recent months, though the organization notes that significant room for further gains remains, particularly on reliability under worst-case conditions where a single unsafe or incorrect answer can outweigh the benefit of many correct ones. Separately, Artificial Analysis provides vendor-neutral benchmarking of models across providers, giving buyers a cost and performance comparison that does not rely on vendor claims.

On the vendor side, KLAS Research has tracked healthcare IT since 1996 by collecting direct feedback from executives, physicians, nurses, and administrators rather than from vendors, producing what it describes as candid performance data on clinical AI solutions. Rock Health tracks the capital flows into digital health, functioning as the standard record of where venture funding lands across clinical AI categories. Together these two organizations offer a buyer the clearest independent view of which vendors perform in practice and where investment is concentrating, though the specific funding figures and vendor rankings from their most recent reports are not reproduced in the material available here.

The governance frame comes from the World Health Organization, whose guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health is the reference document for member-state health systems. That report identifies ethical challenges and risks, articulates six consensus principles for ensuring AI works to the public benefit, and calls for design and deployment to put human rights and ethics at the center, holding both public and private stakeholders accountable to the healthcare workers and communities affected. For any organization deciding whether to deploy, the WHO framework, combined with HealthBench scores as a safety floor and KLAS ratings as a real-world performance check, represents the minimum due diligence structure the field has converged on.
